finding: His posting has a single clear sleep trough at 05:00-06:00 ET and two active humps: a late-night burst (00:00-03:00) and a midday block (09:00-14:00). He is NOT a normal-hours poster, his single busiest clock hour is 1 AM ET.
metric: Trough 05:00 ET = 2.00% of counting posts (n=237) vs peak 01:00 ET = 7.11% (n=842), a 3.5x peak/trough ratio. Late-night 00-03 ET = 26.0% of all counting posts; midday 09-14 ET = 31.4%; the 05-07 ET sleep window holds just 7.3%. Baseline if posting were uniform across 24h = 4.17%/hr.
how_computed: Filtered counts_main_feed==True (11,850 posts), converted ms->America/New_York, grouped by ET hour, computed each hour's share of total. n per hour ranges 237-842 over 294 days.
actionable_for_pacing: High: lets you weight the time-of-day expected-arrival curve. Posts arriving 05:00-07:00 ET are near-zero, so a flat count entering that window is very likely to hold; a count entering the 00-03 ET or 09-14 ET blocks should be projected upward.

finding: His last counting post before the long overnight gap (bedtime) clusters tightly around 03:00 ET, with a median ~6.3h sleep gap and a wake/resume near 09:00 ET. This is a stable daily anchor: the day's activity effectively pauses around 3 AM and resumes mid-morning.
metric: Median bedtime 03:03 ET, mean 03:11 ET, IQR 01:46-04:11 ET (n=257 detected nights). Median overnight gap 377 min (6.28h), median wake hour 09:00 ET. Bedtime-hour mode is 02:00-04:00 ET (158 of 257 nights, 61%).
how_computed: Per ET calendar date, found the largest gap >=180 min whose following post lands 03:00-12:00 ET (overnight sleep), took the pre-gap post as bedtime; circular-adjusted post-midnight hours before taking median/IQR.
actionable_for_pacing: High: by his ~3 AM bedtime the noon-ET market day is ~65% locked (see pacing finding). After the last post before the gap, expect a multi-hour dead zone, so a near-deadline count that reaches 3 AM ET with the market still open is unlikely to move much until ~9 AM ET.

dimension: cumulative share vs hours into noon-ET market window
finding: Within the Polymarket noon-ET to noon-ET window his cumulative count accrues on a stable S-curve. The day is only loosely pinned early (corr 0.57 at 3h) but tightens fast after his evening/overnight run. This curve is the single most useful pacing tool: it converts a partial count + clock time into a projected final.
metric: Median cumulative share of final noon-day total by hours-into-window: 3h(3pm)=13.3%, 6h(6pm)=24.1%, 9h(9pm)=34.3%, 12h(12am)=43.6%, 15h(3am)=65.4%, 18h(6am)=78.9%, 21h(9am)=87.4%. Implied projection multiplier (final/partial, median): 6.0x at 3h, 2.9x at 9h, 2.27x at 12h, 1.53x at 15h, 1.14x at 21h. Partial-to-final correlation rises 0.57(3h)->0.68(9-12h)->0.80(15h)->0.93(21h).
how_computed: Built noon-anchored market day (ts minus 12h, floored to date); for each day counted posts before cutoff h, divided by that day's final total; took median share and final/partial multiplier across 292 full days; corr = Pearson(partial,final).
actionable_for_pacing: Very high, this IS the pacing engine. Multiply the current count by the multiplier for the current hours-into-window to project the close. Confidence widens early (multiplier 6x at 3h is noisy) and tightens after midnight ET (1.5x at 3am, 1.14x by 9am).

pattern: Bursts are the norm, not the exception
finding: Defining a burst as >=6 counting posts inside any 60-min window (overlapping windows merged into episodes), Elon runs ~2.2 bursts/day (~15.4/week). 74% of all counting posts land inside a burst, so day/2-day totals are essentially a count of how many bursts fired, not a smooth drip.
metric: 643 burst episodes over 292 days = 2.20/day (15.4/wk). 8,793 of 11,850 counting posts (74.2%) are in-burst. Baseline mean rate is only 1.69 posts/hr, so a burst is ~4x the background hourly rate sustained for an hour.
how_computed: Filtered counts_main_feed==True (n=11,850). Two-pointer count of posts in [t_i, t_i+60min) per post; posts with count>=6 'trigger'; merged overlapping trigger-windows into episodes. Span Sep 1 2025 -> Jun 20 2026.
actionable_for_pacing: A weekly/2-day count is best modeled as (number of bursts in window) x (avg burst size ~13.7) + sparse background. Predict the count by predicting burst arrivals, not per-hour Poisson draws.

finding: A typical burst is ~11 posts over ~58 min, but the tail is fat: max burst was 87 posts over ~6 hours. Mean size (13.7) sits above median (11) because of long mega-bursts. Once a burst is live, posts arrive every ~2 min (median).
metric: Burst size: mean 13.7, median 11, max 87. Duration: mean 65.2 min, median 57.7 min, max 355 min. Within-burst inter-arrival: median 2.2 min, mean 5.1 min, p90 13.8 min.
how_computed: Per merged episode: size = posts between first and last trigger-covered index; duration = last_ts - first_ts; within-burst gaps = np.diff of in-episode timestamps.
actionable_for_pacing: If a burst is detected live, expect ~11 more posts over the next hour as a median case (and budget for the 87-post tail). For intra-window nowcasting, a burst in progress means the count is about to jump ~11, fast.

finding: Gaps between consecutive posts are massively short-skewed vs a Poisson process at the same mean rate. Short gaps occur 4-7x more often than random. This is the cleanest proof the process is self-exciting, not memoryless.
metric: Median gap 3.4 min. P(gap<2min)=0.380 vs Poisson 0.055 = 6.96x excess; P(gap<5min)=0.577 vs 0.131 = 4.40x; P(gap<10min)=0.693 vs 0.245 = 2.83x. Hourly counts are overdispersed: var/mean = 6.57 (Poisson=1).
how_computed: Inter-event gaps from sorted timestamps. Poisson expectation = 1-exp(-rate*cut) using observed mean rate (1/35.6min). Dispersion from hourly resample variance/mean.
actionable_for_pacing: Do NOT model the daily count as Poisson(rate) - it will badly understate variance. Use a clustered/overdispersed model (negative-binomial or Hawkes). Confidence bands from a Poisson assumption are ~2.5x too narrow.

finding: Right after any post, another post within 10 min is 5x more likely than at a random time. Activity begets activity on a minutes timescale.
metric: P(>=1 post within 10 min of a post)=0.693 vs P(within 10 min of a random reference time)=0.137 -> 5.08x lift.
how_computed: searchsorted on [t,t+10min] for each real post vs for n random uniform timestamps across the span (control). Lift = ratio of the two conditional probabilities.
actionable_for_pacing: Live signal: any new tweet sharply raises the odds of more imminently. Useful for real-time end-of-window nowcasting, but this is a minutes-scale effect, not a multi-hour predictor.

pattern: Early burst predicts a heavy day
finding: The single most useful pacing signal: if a burst starts before noon ET, that calendar day ends with roughly double the posts. Quiet mornings stay quiet.
metric: Days with a pre-noon-ET burst: mean 44.9 / median 39 posts (n=234). Days without: mean 22.4 / median 22 (n=60). P(above-median day | early burst)=0.59 vs 0.13 without (base 0.50). Overall daily mean 40.3, median 36.
how_computed: Tagged each ET calendar date by whether any burst episode started before 12:00 ET; compared day totals across the two groups.
actionable_for_pacing: Best daily nowcast lever. By noon ET, presence/absence of a burst splits the day into ~45-post vs ~22-post regimes. Bake an early-burst flag into the daily projection.

pattern: First-6h of the 2-day window predicts the 48h total
finding: For the Polymarket noon-ET 2-day auction window, the post count in just the first 6 hours correlates 0.60 with the full 48h total. A hot open ~44% more posts by close.
metric: 147 noon-ET 48h windows: corr(first-6h count, 48h total)=0.60. Windows with above-median first-6h: 48h mean 96.2 / median 86; below-median: mean 66.8 / median 62.5.
how_computed: Anchored 48h windows every 2 days at noon ET. Per window: total posts and first-6h posts. Pearson corr + median split on first-6h.
actionable_for_pacing: Directly usable for 2-day auction nowcasting: 6 hours into the window you can already shift the projected 48h total up/down by ~30-45% based on the opening pace. Stronger and earlier than waiting for the full day.

finding: Self-excitation also operates day-to-day: a busy day predicts a busy next day, and the effect persists ~2-3 days. This is real beyond chance, unlike the hourly ACF it is NOT a clock artifact.
metric: Day-level ACF: lag1=0.388, lag2=0.398, lag3=0.255, lag7=0.275. Shuffle null lag1 mean -0.003 sd 0.059 -> z=6.6, p<0.001. P(next busy|busy)=0.62 vs P(next busy|quiet)=0.38 (base 0.50, 1.24x).
how_computed: Daily counts over continuous date range (missing days=0). ACF at lags 1/2/3/7. Null = 1,000 full-permutation shuffles of the daily series.
actionable_for_pacing: Carry yesterday's level forward: a heavy day raises the prior for today and tomorrow. For weekly counts this means days are positively correlated, so weekly totals swing more than independent-day models predict - another reason to use an overdispersed weekly model.

pattern: Pent-up demand is FALSE — quiet does not predict a burst
finding: A long awake quiet stretch does NOT trigger a catch-up burst right after. The opposite is mildly true: after quiet, the very next gap is longer and an immediate burst is LESS likely than normal. Quiet clusters with quiet, it does not rebound.
metric: Post the breaking tweet that ends a >2h awake gap (n=672), posts in the next 120min avg 7.06 vs an hour+weekday-matched control of 7.46 -> ratio 0.95x (and 0.87x at 60min). For >6h quiet (n=82): 8.20 vs 8.34 ctrl = 0.98x. Strict burst test: P(>=4 posts in 10min) right after quiet = 17.9% (>2h) / 14.6% (>6h) vs 27.8% control — quiet makes an immediate burst RARER, not likelier. Median next gap after a >2h gap is 5.4min vs 3.3min after a short gap.
how_computed: counts_main_feed==True only, gaps from ms epoch diff. 'Awake' = gap does not overlap the ET 03:00-08:00 sleep window. Treatment = posts whose preceding gap exceeds threshold and is awake; counted posts (incl. the breaking post) in a fixed window after. Control = all other awake posts, expected count matched on ET hour-of-day (and separately on weekday+hour); ratios consistent across both controls and 60/120min windows.
actionable_for_pacing: Do NOT model a 'he's been quiet, expect a catch-up surge' bump into the 2-day/weekly count. There is no rebound. A quiet morning forecasts a quiet day, so a low running count should LOWER your projected total, not raise it on catch-up logic. This kills a tempting but wrong overlay.

pattern: Posting is positively autocorrelated (sticky), not mean-reverting
dimension: persistence of pace across gaps and days
finding: Pace is sticky at every timescale. Busy begets busy, quiet begets quiet. There is no compensation mechanism pulling him back to an average.
metric: Lag-1 autocorrelation of log inter-post gaps = +0.136 (n=11,848). Day-to-day count autocorrelation = +0.39. After a bottom-quartile day (<=24 posts) next-day mean = 31.8; after a top-quartile day (>=49) next-day mean = 52.8; overall day mean = 40.3 — a 21-post spread driven purely by yesterday.
how_computed: Daily counts grouped by ET calendar date (asfreq D, missing=0). Pearson autocorr on consecutive days and on log-gaps. Quartile-conditioned next-day means.
actionable_for_pacing: Use yesterday's count as a real prior for today. A naive 'regress to the 40/day mean' will be wrong on both tails. For a 2-day auction, the two days are correlated (+0.39), so a hot day-1 meaningfully raises the expected 2-day total rather than borrowing from day-2.

pattern: Morning pace strongly predicts the full-day total
finding: How much he has posted by noon ET is a very strong predictor of where the day lands. By noon he has typically done ~55% of the day.
metric: corr(posts before noon ET, full-day count) = 0.868 (n=294 days). Linear fit: full_day ~= 1.24 * (count_by_noon) + 11.9. Mean AM share of the day = 0.55.
how_computed: Per ET-day split posts at the noon-ET boundary; correlated the pre-noon count against the full-day count; OLS line fit; AM/full ratio averaged per day.
actionable_for_pacing: This is the single best live lever. Mid-auction, read his count-so-far and project the remainder with full ~= 1.24*am + 12 (or scale by the ~55% AM share once you pass noon ET). Far more reliable than any quiet/burst signal for nowcasting the 2-day or weekly total.

pattern: Clear sleep trough at ET 04:00-08:00; most quiet is just sleep
dimension: gap structure / sleep vs awake separation
finding: The bulk of long gaps are sleep, not behavioral pauses. He is busiest after midnight ET (00:00-03:00 are peak hours), with a sharp trough 04:00-08:00 ET. Awake gaps are short and tight.
metric: Per-ET-hour volume troughs at 05:00 (237 posts) vs peak 01:00 (842). Awake gaps (n=9,570): median 3.3min, p90 80min, p95 157min, max 14.6h. Sleep-overlap gaps (n=2,279): p90 330min, max 25.0h. Only 82 of 9,570 awake gaps exceed 6h (0.9%). Longest stretches almost all start in the 02:00-06:00 ET pre-sleep hours.
how_computed: Hour-of-day histogram in ET on counting posts. Gaps classified sleep vs awake by overlap with the daily ET 03:00-08:00 window; percentiles computed per class. Top-15 longest gaps listed with ET start time.
actionable_for_pacing: When projecting remaining posts in an auction window, discount the ET 04:00-08:00 block to near-zero — it is structural downtime, not a signal. A long gap that started near 04:00 ET is just sleep and carries no predictive meaning for a rebound; do not treat it as a 'quiet regime' input.

finding: Of the tweets that count toward the Polymarket auction (counts_main_feed=True), reposts and quotes make up ~93%. Replies, which are 40% of his raw activity, almost entirely DON'T count (they're not main-feed). So the auction count is essentially a repost+quote machine, not an 'original thoughts' machine.
metric: Counted feed (n=11,850): repost 57.3%, quote 35.8%, original 5.6%, reply 1.4%. Raw feed (n=19,601) for contrast: reply 40.4%, repost 34.6%, quote 21.6%, original 3.4%. Source: type.value_counts on counts_main_feed==True.
how_computed: df['counts_main_feed']==True, then df['type'].value_counts(normalize=True). Raw-feed control = same on full df.
actionable_for_pacing: When projecting the weekly/2-day count, model reposts+quotes as the driver; ~93% of every counted tweet is one of those two. Reply spikes in the raw feed are mostly noise (they don't add to the auction number).

pattern: Mix is stable over time and across volume
finding: The post-type mix barely moves month to month or between quiet and loud days. The 'reposts on quiet days, originals on loud days' hypothesis is essentially false here. Loud days are just more of everything in roughly the same proportions; quotes scale a touch faster than reposts.
metric: Monthly repost-share mean 56.0%, std 5.8%, CV=0.103 (very stable). Quiet vs loud days (median split at 36/day): repost 58.6%->56.8%, quote 32.9%->36.5%, original 6.9%->5.4% (all deltas <=3.6pp). Per-type fraction-vs-total-volume Pearson r all weak: quote +0.178, original -0.170, reply -0.105, repost -0.067.
how_computed: Daily counts by type on counted feed; per-day type fractions; corrcoef(total, fraction). Quiet/loud = median split of daily total. Monthly CV = std/mean of monthly repost share.
actionable_for_pacing: Treat the mix as a constant (~57% repost / ~36% quote). Don't try to infer 'a quiet day will be repost-heavy' to adjust a projection. A single blended-rate model is fine; mix-conditioning adds nothing.

pattern: Intraday partial count is the real signal, not the mix
finding: The single most predictive thing for the final daily count is just how many counted tweets have already landed by midday. Mix tells you nothing the running tally doesn't. About 57% of a day's counted tweets are in by noon ET.
metric: Pre-noon-ET counted total vs full-day total: r=0.867 (n=293 days). Pre-noon mean 23.0 vs full-day mean 40.4 => ~57% of the day's count arrives before noon ET.
how_computed: Split counted feed at hour_et<12, daily partial total vs full daily total, corrcoef.
actionable_for_pacing: For live 2-day/weekly pacing, lean on the running partial count (extrapolate the ~57%-by-noon curve), NOT on the post-type breakdown. By noon ET you can pin the day's count with r~0.87. This is the dimension that actually moves a forecast.

pattern: Threads are short, rare, and not tweetstorm-driven
finding: He barely threads. Real self-reply chains are uncommon and short (mostly 2 posts). There is no 'long tweetstorm' regime inflating counts. The longest self-reply thread in 10 months was 6 of his own posts.
metric: self_reply tweets: 160 (0.82% of all 19,601), on 112 of 294 active days. Self-reply threads: 147 chains, mean 2.6 / median 2 / max 6 elon posts. All-conversation grouping: of 18,847 conversation_ids only 559 have >1 elon post (432 of those are just 2); absolute max 8.
how_computed: self_reply==True counts; group by conversation_id for chains containing a self_reply; size distribution.
actionable_for_pacing: No tweetstorm tail to model. You don't need a special high-count regime for threads. Note: all 160 self_reply tweets ARE counts_main_feed=True, so each thread post does add to the auction count (unlike normal replies, which don't count).

pattern: Engagement gradient: original > quote >> reply >> repost
finding: Engagement is wildly type-dependent. Originals and quotes are the high-reach posts; reposts get almost no native engagement (likes on a repost attach to the original). Self-replies in a thread get ~2x the engagement of normal replies.
metric: Median like / median impr by type: original 96,458 / 23.6M; quote 76,205 / 15.5M; reply 2,589 / 116,511; repost 0 / 66. Self-reply vs normal reply (within replies): median like 4,833 vs 2,553, median impr 650,282 vs 113,856.
how_computed: groupby('type') median and mean of like/impr/rt/reply; within type=='reply' split on self_reply.
actionable_for_pacing: Engagement does NOT help predict the count (a 57%-repost feed is engagement-poor by construction). If anything, don't weight a projection by engagement. Only relevance: a thread/self-reply gets outsized reach, consistent with it marking a more-engaged day (ties to the thread-day-runs-hotter finding).

dimension: SpaceX launches (exact liftoff time, net) — routine Starlink
finding: In the 2 hours right after a Starlink liftoff, Elon's counting-post rate jumps ~1.4x above his normal pace, driven almost entirely by reposts of the SpaceX launch. The burst is real and tightly time-locked: it appears only in [0,+2h] and is gone by +2h. There is NO elevation in the hour before launch and NO elevation in [+2h,+6h].
metric: Starlink [0,+2h]: 2.40 posts/hr observed vs 1.68/hr random-anchor control (z=+2.9, p(rand>=obs)=0.010). Reposts specifically: 1.53/hr vs 0.97/hr baseline = 1.59x. Pre-window [-60,0]: 1.52/hr (z=-0.5, none). Decay window [+2h,+6h]: 1.63/hr (z=-0.3, none). 38% of Starlink launches (39/102) get a confirmed SpaceX-themed repost within 2h; ~59% get any repost.
how_computed: Filtered counts_main_feed==True (n=11,850 counting posts, Sep 2025->Jun 2026, baseline 1.69/hr, gap-CV 2.67). Anchored on exact net liftoff times from spacex_launches.json (102 Starlink, 27 other, 2 Starship in window). Computed posts/hr in fixed minute-windows relative to each liftoff; control = 200 sets of random in-window anchors (same n), reported as z and empirical p. Decomposed the burst by post type and grepped repost text for SpaceX/Starlink/Falcon to confirm it is launch reposts.
actionable_for_pacing: Small but real upward nudge. Each Starlink launch adds ~+1.4 counting posts concentrated in the 2h after liftoff. At ~0.35 launches/day this is only ~+0.5 posts/day on average, so it barely moves a weekly/2-day total UNLESS several launches cluster in the auction window. For a 2-day count: pull that window's scheduled liftoff times and add ~+1.4 per launch landing inside the window (front-load them into the 2h post-liftoff bin, not spread evenly).

finding: How many main-feed posts Elon has put out by 11am ET strongly predicts his full-day total. By 11am ET roughly 55% of the day's posts are already out, and a by-3pm ET checkpoint nails it even tighter. This is the single most actionable lever for predicting the day's count before it closes.
metric: corr(posts-by-11am-ET, full-day total) = 0.868; corr(posts-by-3pm-ET, full-day) = 0.922. Mean share of day done by 11am = 55%, by 3pm = 70%. Linear nowcast: full_day ~= 1.24*(by-11am) + 11.9. n=294 days.
how_computed: counts_main_feed==True only; ms->UTC->America/New_York; bucketed each post by ET hour; cumulative count through hour 11 (and hour 14) per day vs full-day total; Pearson corr + np.polyfit slope.
actionable_for_pacing: Direct intraday estimator: at 11am ET multiply running count by ~1.8 (or use 1.24*x+11.9) to project the full day; at 3pm ET multiply by ~1.4. Tighten a 2-day-bracket position once the morning pace is known rather than waiting for market close.

finding: Daily volume is persistent but strongly mean-reverting. A heavy posting day is reliably followed by a lighter one and vice-versa, so today's count is itself a predictor of tomorrow's direction.
metric: AR(1) on daily count = 0.390 (noise band +/-0.114, so clearly real). After a top-20% volume day, next-day change = -21.0 posts (n=58). After a bottom-20% day, next-day change = +14.3 posts (n=59). Control: same metric, opposite tails move in opposite directions.
how_computed: Daily main-feed counts; pandas autocorr lag-1; split days into top/bottom quintile by volume and measured mean(next_day - today) for each tail.
actionable_for_pacing: When projecting a 2-day bracket, regress today's count toward the ~40/day mean for tomorrow rather than extrapolating a hot day flat. After an extreme day, bias the next-day estimate ~21 posts lower (hot) or ~14 higher (cold).

finding: His baseline rate is not stationary: it doubled into a Jan 2026 peak then bled back down. Any pacing model anchored on a fixed daily mean drifts; the running baseline must be re-estimated monthly.
metric: Posts/day by month: Sep 31.8, Oct 35.7, Nov 31.5, Dec 53.8, Jan 68.1 (peak), Feb 44.2, Mar 42.8, Apr 35.2, May 26.8, Jun 30.4. Jan was 2.1x the May trough. Overall daily mean 40.3, median 36.5, std 22.7 (range 3-138).
how_computed: Grouped main-feed posts by ET month and by date; monthly total / active days.
actionable_for_pacing: Do not hardcode a 40/day prior. Use a trailing 14-30 day mean as the regime baseline; current regime (May-Jun 2026) is ~27-30/day, well below the lifetime mean.

finding: Output is extremely clumpy, not a smooth Poisson stream. Most posts arrive in tight bursts minutes apart, with long quiet gaps between sessions. A naive constant-rate (Poisson) pacing model will be miscalibrated.
metric: Inter-post gap median 3.4 min, mean 35.6 min (heavy tail). 38% of gaps <2 min, 57.7% of posts land within 5 min of the prior one; only 4.4% of gaps exceed 4 hours. Burst-share corr with same-day volume = 0.684.
how_computed: Main-feed posts sorted by ms; diff of timestamps -> gap minutes; quantiles and threshold shares; per-day burst share = fraction of gaps <5 min, correlated to daily volume.
actionable_for_pacing: Model the day as a small number of burst sessions, not a flat hourly rate. Variance of any short-window projection is high mid-burst; wait for a burst to close before re-projecting. Burst-share is mostly a proxy for total volume, so it adds little beyond the count itself.

dimension: projection uncertainty (final/partial multiplier dispersion by cutoff)
finding: The existing pacing curve gives a single median multiplier per hour, but the real spread is huge early and only collapses late. This converts the pacing engine from a point estimate into a calibrated confidence band, which is what you actually need to size a bet near a deadline.
metric: final/partial multiplier (median, p10, p90) by hours-into-window: 3h = 6.0x [2.78-27.0], 6h = 4.06x [2.04-11.7], 9h = 2.89x [1.61-7.45], 12h = 2.27x [1.35-5.63], 15h = 1.52x [1.07-2.81], 18h = 1.26x [1.00-1.95], 21h = 1.14x [1.00-1.57]. The p90/p10 ratio shrinks from ~10x at 3h to ~1.6x at 21h. n grows 240->294 days as cutoffs lengthen.
how_computed: For each noon-anchored market day and each cutoff h, computed final/partial multiplier (final total divided by count before cutoff, days with partial>0). Took median, 10th, and 90th percentile of that ratio across all days per cutoff.
actionable_for_pacing: Very high: attach these p10/p90 bands to every projection. Pre-midnight (<=12h in) the upside tail is enormous (p90 multiplier 5.6x at midnight) so never treat an early count as near-final. After ~3am ET (15h+) the band tightens to roughly +-1.5x, which is where confident deadline sizing becomes safe. Use the band, not the median, to decide bet size.

finding: Volume is momentum-driven: a busy day tends to follow a busy day. A 3-day trailing average is a usable prior for the next noon-day total before any of that day's posts arrive, which sets the starting expectation the intraday curve then updates.
metric: Lag-1 autocorrelation (yesterday->today) = 0.440. 3-day trailing mean -> today correlation = 0.515 (R^2 = 0.265, so the recent baseline alone explains ~27% of next-day variance). Noon-day totals: mean 40.4, median 36, std 21.4, 10/25/50/75/90 pctiles = 16/25/36/51/69.
how_computed: Grouped counting posts into noon-anchored market days (292 full days), computed Pearson lag-1 autocorr and correlation of a shift(1) 3-day rolling mean against the actual day.
actionable_for_pacing: Moderate: use the trailing-3-day mean as the Bayesian prior at window open (0h), then let the intraday pacing curve dominate as real posts arrive. Don't treat days as i.i.d. around the global mean, recent days carry real signal.

finding: An active hour predicts the next hour being active (lift up to 2.3x at burst-level), but most of the raw hourly autocorrelation is just Elon's daily clock. After controlling for time-of-day, an active hour still adds a genuine but modest +12 percentage points to next-hour activity beyond what the clock alone predicts.
metric: Raw lag-1 hourly ACF=0.240. P(next active|active)=0.542 vs base 0.396 (1.37x); at >=6 threshold 0.238 vs 0.102 (2.33x). After circadian control: among active-now hours, actual next-active 0.542 vs circadian-only expected 0.426 = +11.7pts excess. Day-shuffle null ACF=0.234 (z=3.1, p<0.005), so only ~0.006 of the 0.240 ACF is beyond-clock memory.
how_computed: Hourly resample over continuous span, empty hours=0. Circadian baseline = P(active) by ET hour-of-day; predicted next-hour prob from its hour-of-day only; excess = actual - circadian. Day-shuffle null permutes intact 24h ET day-vectors (500 reps).
actionable_for_pacing: Hour-level momentum is real but small once you account for the clock. For pacing, the dominant hourly structure is circadian (use hour-of-day priors); add only a modest +12pt bump for 'currently active'. Don't overweight a single active hour as a trend.

pattern: Burst arrival timing skews overnight ET
finding: Bursts do not start uniformly. They cluster in late-night/early-morning ET (midnight-2am) plus a 9-11am ET block; only ~39% start during US business hours. This reflects Elon's posting clock (heavy late-night) and is the circadian backbone behind the hourly ACF.
metric: Top burst-start ET hours: 0:00 (53), 1:00 (50), 9:00 (45), 2:00 (40), 11:00 (40), 10:00 (34). Only 38.9% of bursts start 9a-5p ET. Mean gap end-of-burst -> next-burst-start = 9.9h (median 7.1h).
how_computed: Hour-of-day (ET) of each episode's start timestamp; value_counts. Business-hours share = fraction starting 9-17 ET.
actionable_for_pacing: Use ET hour-of-day burst priors when projecting an in-progress window: a window opening at noon ET still has the heavy overnight burst block ahead of it, so don't extrapolate a quiet afternoon linearly. The ~7h median inter-burst gap sets the natural pacing clock.

pattern: Quote count is the high-variance, slightly-leading component
finding: Of the components, the absolute QUOTE count is the most informative for tomorrow's total, marginally beating today's total itself. But the edge over just using today's total is tiny. Reposts are the stable base; quotes are where the day-to-day spikiness lives.
metric: Today->tomorrow total: today_total r=+0.390; today_quote_abs r=+0.419; today_repost_abs r=+0.338; today_original_abs r=+0.055. OLS R2 for tomorrow: total-only 0.152, quote-only 0.176, total+quote 0.177 (quote adds ~0.025 R2 over total). Loud vs quiet absolute scaling: quote 2.65x, repost 2.38x, reply 1.86x, original 1.80x.
how_computed: Shifted daily total by -1; corrcoef of today's per-type abs/frac vs tomorrow total; numpy lstsq OLS for incremental R2.
actionable_for_pacing: If you want one leading number for a next-day/AR projection, today's quote count is marginally better than today's total, and quotes are the variance you most need to forecast. But the gain is small (R2 +0.025); not worth a complex model. Reposts are a near-constant base rate you can almost treat as a floor.

pattern: Thread days run hotter, mostly non-mechanically
finding: Days where he self-replies tend to be higher-total days, and most of that lift is NOT just the extra thread posts. A self-reply is a weak tell that it's an engaged/active day.
metric: Thread days (n=112) mean total 45.4 vs non-thread (n=182) 37.2 = 1.22x, Mann-Whitney p=0.0006. Removing the self_reply posts themselves (avg 1.4/day, all of which count): residual 43.9 vs 37.2 = 1.18x, p=0.004. So ~1.4 of the +8.2 lift is mechanical, ~6.8 is genuine.
how_computed: Flag days with >=1 self_reply; Mann-Whitney U one-sided on daily total; re-test on total minus self_reply count to strip the mechanical part.
actionable_for_pacing: A self-reply landing intraday is a mild upward nudge on the day's projection (~+18% over a no-thread baseline, beyond the mechanical post). Minor secondary signal; the partial-count curve still dominates.

dimension: Tesla earnings calls (exact start 17:30 ET, web-confirmed) — Musk participates live
finding: Elon goes completely silent on his counting feed for the ~75-90 minutes he is live on a Tesla earnings call, then bounces back above baseline right after. Across all 3 in-window calls (Q3-25 Oct22, Q4-25 Jan28, Q1-26 Apr22) he posted ZERO counting posts during the call window. His silence gap spanned 194-253 minutes around the call vs a typical 6-minute evening gap (a 12x+ stretch). The post-call bounce roughly cancels the suppression, so the NET effect on the day's total is near zero.
metric: During [0,+75min]: 0 posts on all 3 calls (raw [0,0,0]); Poisson P(X=0) under baseline = 0.0018 (expected ~6.3 posts). Random control during-window = 1.63/hr. Pre [-60,0]: 0.33/hr. After [+75,+195min]: 2.50/hr (avg 5.0 posts vs 3.4 baseline, +1.6). Silence gaps: Q4-25 194 min, Q1-26 253 min vs 6-min median evening gap. n=3 calls so the during-window z is only -0.9 alone, but the pooled Poisson zero is significant.
how_computed: Found the 3 Tesla earnings calls in elon_events_2026.json, web-confirmed start time 5:30 PM ET (4:30 CT) for Q1-2026, applied DST-correct ET->UTC. Tested pre/during/after windows in posts/hr vs 2000-rep random-anchor control, plus a pooled Poisson test of observed=0 against his baseline rate over 3x75min. Measured per-call last-post-before / first-post-after silence gaps.
actionable_for_pacing: Use as a within-window TIMING shaper, not a daily-total mover. When a Tesla earnings call sits inside the auction window, expect a hard ~75-90 min zero-post hole starting 17:30 ET on call day, immediately followed by an above-baseline catch-up burst. The day's total is ~unchanged (suppression ~2 posts, post-bounce ~+1.6), so do not subtract from a 2-day/weekly count — just don't expect posts during the call hour. n=3 limits confidence; revisit as more calls log.

finding: Consecutive 2-day post totals are moderately correlated, so the prior 2-day block carries real information about the next one. Useful because the tradeable brackets are 2-day windows.
metric: corr(this 2-day sum, next 2-day sum) = 0.524. 2-day sum: mean 81, median 73, std 38. n~294 days.
how_computed: Daily counts reindexed to daily freq (missing days=0), 2-day rolling sum, correlated against the sum shifted -2 days.
actionable_for_pacing: Seed the 2-day-bracket projection with the previous 2-day total (which alone explains ~27% of variance), then adjust for mean reversion and the intraday nowcast as the window fills.

finding: His reply activity tracks his same-day main-feed volume but does NOT lead it. On an active day he replies more and posts more together; today's reply count gives almost no edge on tomorrow.
metric: corr(today reply-count, today main-vol) = 0.489; corr(today reply-count, NEXT-day main-vol) = 0.132 (collapses to noise). Control: same-day vs lagged on the same series.
how_computed: Replies (type=='reply', excluded from main feed) counted per day; correlated with same-day and next-day main-feed counts.
actionable_for_pacing: Reply count is a useful real-time activity confirmation within the day (a quiet reply morning = quiet posting morning), but it is not a next-day predictor. Fold it into the intraday nowcast, not the forward forecast.

finding: His peak output is overnight ET (12am-3am), with a dead zone at 5-6am ET. About a quarter of each day's posts land in the 0-4am ET overnight block, and that share has been fairly stable (recently easing from ~28% to ~20%).
metric: Hour-of-day ET peaks at 1am (842), 2am (796), 3am (739); trough at 5am (237) and 6am (262). Overnight 0-4am ET share by month: 24-28% through Apr 2026, dropping to 20% in May-Jun 2026.
how_computed: Main-feed posts by ET hour (full-period histogram) and by month for the 0-3am block as a share of monthly total.
actionable_for_pacing: A 2-day window that is light by US daytime can still fill heavily overnight ET. Don't write off a low count before the early-morning ET block; weight the overnight catch-up at ~20-25% of remaining expected output.

finding: The main feed is dominated by reposts and quotes, not original tweets, and that mix is remarkably stable month to month. Original tweets are a thin, near-constant slice. So 'counts_main_feed' volume is mostly amplification behavior, which is cheaper/faster for him to produce and explains the burstiness.
metric: Type share of main feed (stable across Sep 2025-Jun 2026): repost ~52-60%, quote ~30-42%, original only 4-9%. Pure originals never exceed 9% of any month.
how_computed: Per-month type counts among counts_main_feed posts, normalized to row percentages.
actionable_for_pacing: Because ~90%+ of the count is reposts/quotes (low-effort, burstable), the count can spike fast on a news cycle without him 'writing' more. Treat originals as a near-constant ~2-5/day floor and model the variable mass as repost/quote amplification.

dimension: intra-window leading indicator (latency to first counting post)
finding: How long after the noon-ET window opens his FIRST counting post arrives is a clean early predictor of the day's final total, available the moment that first post lands. A fast first post (within ~3h of noon) means a normal-to-heavy ~44-post day; if no counting post has arrived 6+ hours into the window, the day almost always finishes light (~20).
metric: hrs-to-first-post vs final-total corr = -0.348 (n=292 market-days). First post <=3h into window: mean 43.6 / median 40 (n=239). First post >6h into window: mean 20.6 / median 20 (n=14). So a slow open roughly halves the expected close.
how_computed: Built noon-ET-anchored market days (ts - 12h, floored to date). For each day took the first counts_main_feed==True post, computed hours from the 12:00 ET window-open (DST-correct tz_localize) to that post; correlated against the day's final counting total; split at 3h and 6h. Dropped the partial first/last day.
actionable_for_pacing: High and EARLY: this fires before the intraday S-curve has data. At window open, start a stopwatch. If 6h pass with zero counting posts, hard-discount the projection toward ~20. A first post inside 3h restores the normal ~44 prior. Combine with the early-burst flag for a stronger pre-3pm nowcast.

pattern: Weekend reshapes the clock (it does not just lower volume)
dimension: hour-of-day SHAPE, weekend vs weekday (phase, not amplitude)
finding: The known ~6% weekend volume dip hides a real STRUCTURAL change: his late-night peak is unchanged, but the weekday midday work-block collapses and shifts into a lazier late-morning and evening. So the time-of-day expected-arrival curve must be SWAPPED on weekends, not just scaled down. Same 1 AM ET peak both, but the daytime profile is materially different.
metric: Busiest clock hour is 01:00 ET on BOTH weekday (6.8%) and weekend (7.9%). 00-03 ET share is flat (weekday 25.9% vs weekend 26.2%). The shift is in daytime: midday 09-14 ET drops weekday 34.5% -> weekend 23.4% (-11pts), while morning 05-08 ET nearly doubles 9.7% -> 15.4% and evening 20-23 ET rises 10.3% -> 13.8%. Weekday/weekend hourly-shape correlation only 0.55. n: weekday 8,609 / weekend 3,241 posts.
how_computed: Filtered counts_main_feed==True, converted ms->America/New_York, split by dayofweek>=5, normalized each group's posts-per-ET-hour to a share, compared block shares and the single busiest hour, and correlated the two 24-hour shape vectors.
actionable_for_pacing: Moderate-high: keep a SEPARATE weekend hour-of-day pacing curve. On weekend windows, expect less accrual through the 9am-2pm block (a flat count there is more likely to hold) and more in the 5-8am and evening hours than the weekday curve implies. Do not model weekends as a simple volume haircut on the weekday shape.

pattern: Weak day-of-week effect (Fri down, Thu up)
finding: Day-of-week barely moves volume. Raw per-day averages span only ~17% (Fri highest at 43.4, Sat lowest at 36.3). After controlling for recent baseline, the only non-trivial residuals are Thursday up and Friday down, and even those are small relative to daily noise.
metric: Per-calendar-day averages (counting posts): Mon 37.1, Tue 40.2, Wed 42.2, Thu 42.0, Fri 43.4, Sat 36.3, Sun 40.8 (each over 42 days). Residual (actual minus 3-day trailing) by noon-day start DOW: Thu +3.4, Fri -3.7, others within +/-1.8. Daily std is 21.4, so a +/-3.5 DOW residual is ~0.16 sigma.
how_computed: Normalized totals by distinct count of each weekday across the span; separately regressed-out the 3-day trailing mean and averaged the residual by the noon-day's start weekday.
actionable_for_pacing: Low: not worth a hard adjustment. At most, nudge projections slightly down on Friday noon-windows and slightly up on Thursday; the effect is dwarfed by intraday pacing and day-to-day momentum.

finding: He posts marginally less on weekends, but the gap is small and within normal day-to-day variation, so it is not a reliable standalone predictor.
metric: Weekday avg 41.0/day (n=8,609 over 210 days) vs weekend avg 38.6/day (n=3,241 over 84 days); ratio 0.941 (weekend ~6% lower). Spread is far inside the daily std of 21.4.
how_computed: Split counting posts into weekday (Mon-Fri) vs weekend (Sat-Sun), divided each total by its distinct calendar-day count, took the ratio.
actionable_for_pacing: Low: a ~6% haircut for weekend windows is defensible but minor. Subsumed by the day-of-week and trailing-mean signals; don't double-count it.

finding: Over the full ~10-month span weekly volume is essentially flat with very high variance, but the most recent stretch runs below the historical average. There is no clean monotonic trend to extrapolate, so any pacing prior should lean on recent weeks rather than the global mean.
metric: 41 full weeks: mean 284.5 posts/week, std 105.9 (CV 37%), range 117-593. OLS slope -0.81 posts/week per week (negligible). First-8-weeks mean 236.4 vs last-8-weeks mean 196.5 (~17% lower recently). Last 12 weeks bounce 129-313 with no direction.
how_computed: Aggregated counting posts into full ISO weeks (W-SUN), dropped partial endpoints, fit OLS trend and compared first-8 vs last-8-week means.
actionable_for_pacing: Low-moderate: don't extrapolate a trend, there isn't one. But because recent weeks run ~17% under the all-time mean, anchor the at-open prior on a trailing window (3-7 days), not the global average, or you will systematically over-project.

pattern: Day-type levers (weekday, weekend, SpaceX launches) barely move the count
dimension: calendar / external-event drivers of daily volume
finding: Daily volume is remarkably flat across day-of-week, weekend vs weekday, and SpaceX launch days. None of these are useful pacing inputs versus the intraday and persistence signals.
metric: Mean count by weekday ranges only 37.1 (Mon) to 43.4 (Fri). Weekend 38.6 vs weekday 41.0 = 0.94x. Launch days (n=120) mean 40.1 vs non-launch 40.4 — effectively identical. Overall daily: mean 40.3, std 22.7, p10 16, p50 36, p90 71, max 138. 2-day rolling: mean 80.8, p10 41, p50 73, p90 133.
how_computed: Counts grouped by ET date, joined to weekday, to launch dates (spacex_launches.json net times converted to ET date). Group means compared.
actionable_for_pacing: Skip weekday/weekend/launch dummies — they add noise, not signal. The day-to-day variance (std 22.7 on a mean of 40) is enormous and is driven by his own momentum (yesterday's count, today's morning pace), not the calendar. Use the persistence + AM-pace signals as your projection backbone and treat the 2-day p10/p50/p90 of 41/73/133 as the empirical band.

finding: Tested the intuitive hypothesis that high-volume days dilute per-tweet engagement. The mean impressions/tweet look ~1.3x higher on low-volume days, but on a rank-correlation test with a clean control it does NOT hold up. There is no reliable engagement signal that predicts volume.
metric: Tercile means suggested low-vol days = 31.4M median impr vs high-vol 24.1M (1.3x). But Spearman(daily vol, median original-tweet impressions) = -0.093, p=0.15, n=247 (not significant). corr(today engagement, next-day vol) = -0.277 also unstable.
how_computed: Engagement from pure originals only (reposts inherit source metrics, so excluded); median impressions/likes per day vs daily count; tercile means AND Spearman rank test with p-value as the control against the mean-driven illusion.
actionable_for_pacing: None reliable. Do not use per-tweet engagement (impressions/likes) as a feature to predict his daily count; the apparent dilution effect is a mean artifact and vanishes under a rank test. Drop it from the pacing model.

pattern: Replies are diffuse, no key interlocutor
finding: His replies spray across a huge rotating set of accounts with no dominant target; the single most-replied account each month is himself (self-reply thread continuations). There is no specific account whose activity could be used as an external trigger for his posting.
metric: 7,911 replies, top single target only 160 of total (~2%); 278-557 distinct reply targets every month; top-target share never exceeds 4% of a month. Most-replied ID 44196397 = Elon's own account (self-threads).
how_computed: type=='reply' grouped by in_reply_to; monthly top-target share and distinct-target count; identified ID 44196397 as Elon himself from its rank as top self-reply target.
actionable_for_pacing: No usable external interlocutor signal. Self-replies are the only meaningful cluster and they are already captured by counts_main_feed (self_reply rule). Do not try to predict his volume off any one account he talks to.

pattern: SpaceX launches do NOT lift whole-window volume (a useful null)
dimension: exogenous event -> bulk count (launches), with random control
finding: The validated 'SpaceX repost within 4h of a launch' effect is real for that ONE repost, but it does NOT translate into a measurable increase in his total counting volume over the surrounding hours. Launch days are not high-count days. This kills a tempting-but-false pacing lever: do not bump a window's projection just because a launch is scheduled.
metric: Posts in +0..6h after ANY launch: mean 10.80 vs random-anchor null 10.03, lift 1.08x, p=0.18 (not significant; n=131). MARQUEE launches (Starship/crewed, n=29): 8.93 vs null 10.24, lift 0.87x, p=0.75 (if anything LOWER). Routine Starlink (n=102): 11.33 vs 10.02, lift 1.13x, p=0.067 (marginal at best).
how_computed: Loaded spacex_launches.json, kept launches inside the data span, counted counts_main_feed posts in [liftoff, liftoff+6h] via searchsorted on epoch-ms. Null = 300 redraws of the same number of random anchor times across the span; reported lift and the share of null means >= observed (empirical p). Split marquee (non-Starlink) vs routine.
actionable_for_pacing: Actionable as a NEGATIVE: ignore the launch calendar for volume projection. The launch signal is a single near-deterministic repost (good for nowcasting that ONE post lands), not a day-level burst trigger. The marquee=lower result warns that a focused launch can even crowd out his usual reposting. Do not add a launch-day multiplier.

finding: Only 2 Starship launches fell in the data window, so routine-vs-marquee cannot be split with any confidence. Both got a repost within 4h (median 84 min), consistent with the Starlink pattern but n is far too small to claim a larger or different marquee response.
metric: Starship n=2; repost-within-4h 2/2, median 84 min. No control test possible at n=2.
how_computed: Same exact-time anchoring on the 2 Starship liftoffs in spacex_launches.json. No statistical test run given n=2.
actionable_for_pacing: Not usable for pacing as a separate class. Treat any in-window Starship launch with the same ~+1.4-post post-liftoff bump as routine Starlink until more marquee events accumulate.

pattern: No exact-time response detectable for other categories
finding: The other plausible exact-time categories (16 single-date podcast/interview/livestream events) carry only a calendar date in the events JSON, no minute-level start time. Without web-looking-up each one, they cannot be anchored at the fine resolution this method requires, and coarse daily windows are swamped by his 2.6x-bursty baseline. No reliable exact-time response was establishable for these from the data provided.
metric: 16 timed-category events with date-only granularity; 0 testable at minute precision without per-event time lookup. Coarse 6h/daily windows give no signal separable from baseline (CV 2.67).
how_computed: Filtered events JSON to podcast/interview/livestream single-date rows; confirmed none carry an exact start time. Did not fabricate anchors. Only Tesla earnings (web-confirmable fixed 17:30 ET) and SpaceX launches (exact net field) had true exact-time anchors.
actionable_for_pacing: Not currently actionable. If a future auction window contains a known long-form appearance (e.g. a 3h Joe Rogan taping), the earnings-call finding suggests a similar quiet-during hole is plausible, but it is unproven here. To make it usable, backfill exact start times for those events, then re-run the same windowed-rate + control test.

pattern: SpaceX launches do not move volume
finding: Tested whether SpaceX launches drive his posting. Routine Starlink launches have zero effect, and the four marquee launches in-window were actually slightly BELOW average. Launch calendars are not a useful pacing input.
metric: Routine Starlink launch-day volume 40.7/day (n=102) vs overall baseline 40.3 (no lift). Marquee launches: launch-day 37.8, day-before 33.5, day-after 26.8 (n=4, below mean, tiny sample). Overall daily mean 40.3.
how_computed: Parsed spacex_launches.json net times -> ET dates; flagged Starlink (routine) vs Starship/crewed (marquee); compared main-feed daily count on launch days vs baseline and adjacent days.
actionable_for_pacing: Drop SpaceX launch dates as a feature. They carry no predictive lift on his daily count over the Sep 2025-Jun 2026 window. Spend the modeling budget on the intraday nowcast and mean-reversion instead.
